extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, philosophy of science, and methodology (readers of Mill's System of Logic)
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing and formulating valid inductions and causal explanations: distinguishing descriptions from explanations, testing competing theories and predictions for consistency, and applying rules about causes, negative conditions, and composition of causes. Emphasizes how scientific induction differs from practical inference and how uniformity of nature functions as a premise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between Description and Explanation (Induction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions merely represent or state the facts (a mode of representing the facts); Explanations (Inductions) ascribe a cause or general law and attempt to account for the phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An account that is only a convenient representation of observed regularities (a Description) may be consistent with multiple representational schemes; an Explanation, which posits a mechanism or law, may be mutually exclusive with alternative explanatory mechanisms. Example: Kepler’s law as a Description vs Newtonian theory as an Explanation. Anti-pattern: treating a mechanistic hypothesis (vortices) as merely a Description when it asserts a physical agent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual Exclusivity of Conflicting Explanations and Predictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Conflicting substantive explanations or predictions about the same fact or event cannot both be true when they assert incompatible mechanisms or outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test competing theories by whether their asserted mechanisms can both obtain; if they posit incompatible physical agents or incompatible laws, they are not both true. Examples: vortices vs Newtonian gravitation; emission vs undulatory theories of light; conflicting predictions of periodicity for a comet. Anti-pattern: asserting that differing analogies or descriptions that merely aid conception equate to alternative true explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific Induction Requires General Propositions (Formalization)
rubrics_metrics.description: In science, inductive inference ordinarily passes through an intermediate general proposition (a general law) because science records general conclusions rather than only instantaneous judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating scientific work, expect explicit generalizations or laws to be stated. In practical affairs, competent inferences may be made without articulate general propositions, but their logical status as inductions remains comparable. Scoring note: prefer explicit formulation of general laws in scientific presentations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniformity of Nature as a Condition of Valid Induction (within Relevant Class)
rubrics_metrics.description: Validity of every induction requires uniformity in the course of nature, but it is sufficient that such uniformity obtain in the particular class of phenomena to which the induction relates, not necessarily throughout all nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the assumed uniformity pertains to the relevant domain (e.g., astronomical phenomena, magnetism). Anti-pattern: demanding universal uniformity across all phenomena when the induction concerns a specific class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction Implies Either Known or Newly Established General Uniformity
rubrics_metrics.description: An inductive conclusion either presupposes that the general uniformity is already known or that the present evidence entitles us now to infer it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging an induction, check whether the general law was treated as antecedently established or whether the evidence is sufficient to establish it now. Clarify which of the two interpretations is intended to avoid paralogisms about the grounds of induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanations Must Identify Mechanisms Compatible with the Law/Observations
rubrics_metrics.description: An explanation consists in ascribing observed phenomena to a general law or mechanism that coheres with other known laws and facts; an explanation that posits incompatible mechanisms is invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the proposed mechanism both accounts for the specific facts and fits into the broader system of laws (e.g., identifying planetary motion with the same law as terrestrial falling). Anti-pattern: treating a hypothesis as explanatory when it merely offers a representational device without commitments about physical agents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply 'Cause' to Informative/Relevant Conditions (Proximate vs Remote Causes)
rubrics_metrics.description: In ordinary discourse, 'cause' is applied to the antecedent condition that the hearer may require to be informed of—the proximate or informative antecedent—rather than to every necessary condition or antecedent state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assigning causal responsibility, prefer proximate conditions that answer the question sought by inquiry (e.g., saying someone died because of poisoning rather than because they had organs). Anti-pattern: indiscriminately labeling all necessary antecedent states as the cause when they add no explanatory information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative Conditions and Absence of Counteracting Causes Can Serve as Causes
rubrics_metrics.description: The absence of counteracting causes (a negative condition) may be legitimately cited as the cause of an effect when it is the relevant informative factor that made the event occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow negative conditions as causal explanations when they uniquely account for the occurrence (e.g., drowning because one cannot swim; death for want of medical advice). Scoring note: ensure the negative condition is not redundant with other obvious conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of Causes (Combination Principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Causes generally compose; the combined action of causes produces combined effects, though apparent exceptions may arise because immediate/mediating collocations reach a threshold beyond which doubling does not double the observed effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating alleged counterexamples (e.g., one spark vs two sparks, dose-response plateaus), analyze immediate vs remote effects and collocations: doubling causative input may double the collocation even if the observed final effect is limited by other constraints. Anti-pattern: concluding failure of causal composition without distinguishing immediate/remote effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cases of Preventive Properties Should Be Analyzed as Absence of Counteracting Agency
rubrics_metrics.description: Properties that appear purely preventive (e.g., opacity blocking light) are not genuine exceptions to causal composition if they can be analyzed as agencies that defeat other agencies; the general formula treating absence of counteracting causes still applies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate underlying relations (structure or interactions) that produce preventive phenomena; treat such cases as compatible with standard causal analysis unless all counteracting agencies are of a wholly different, non-interacting type. Anti-pattern: declaring preventive properties as fundamental exceptions without seeking deeper causal relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical (Tacit) Inductions Can Exhibit Equal Intellectual Merit to Scientific Inductions
rubrics_metrics.description: Inferences made for practical guidance—often without formal generalization—can display intellectual powers equal to those in scientific induction and should not be dismissed simply because they are not expressed as general propositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reviewing applied or practice-oriented work, respect tacitly-held inductions and assess their evidential support and reliability even if the author does not formulate explicit general laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Erroneous Inductions Often Rely on Appeals to Coincidence and A Priori Prejudices
rubrics_metrics.description: Superstitious or erroneous inductions typically justify themselves by selective appeals to coincidental facts and are reinforced by antecedent prejudices of probability that predispose interpretation of experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scrutinize claimed inductive support for confected generalizations: check for selective use of coincidences, unnoticed biases, or antecedent presuppositions that have led to misconstrual of evidence. Example: belief that crops depend on moon increase backed by farmers' repeated but fallacious experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human Actions Are Subject to Causal Analysis (Not Exempt)
rubrics_metrics.description: Human volitions and actions can be treated as following causes (motives, character) in the same way as material events; to say actions necessarily follow character is only to say behavior is predictable from character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In moral or social sciences, evaluate explanations of action in terms of motives and character as causal generalizations that admit predictive force; avoid exempting human will from causal inquiry on purely introspective grounds.
